questions.question_text: Written in expanded form, $4^{3}\times 4^{2}$ is $(4\times4\times4)\times(4\times4)$. Counting the factors, this equals which single power?

options.why: Multiplied the indices instead of counting the total number of factors.
Counted the factors correctly but multiplied the two bases together as well.
Subtracted the indices as though the powers were being divided.

questions.question_text: Expanding $3^{5}\div 3^{2}$ gives $\frac{3\times3\times3\times3\times3}{3\times3}$. After cancelling, this equals which single power?

options.why: Added the indices as though the powers were being multiplied.
Counted the factors that were cancelled instead of the factors left over.
Multiplied the indices as in a power of a power.

questions.question_text: Written in expanded form, $\left(5^{2}\right)^{4}$ is $(5\times5)\times(5\times5)\times(5\times5)\times(5\times5)$. This equals which single power?

options.why: Added the two indices instead of multiplying them.
Kept only the outer index and ignored the power inside the bracket.
Counted the factors correctly but also applied the inner power to the base.

questions.question_text: Expanding shows that a product of powers of the same base is one long string of equal factors. Which statement completes the rule: when multiplying two powers with the same base, ...?

options.text: keep the base and add the indices
keep the base and multiply the indices
options.why: Uses the power-of-a-power rule, where the indices multiply, for a product instead.

options.text: multiply the bases and add the indices
options.why: Assumes each base is used again, but expanding shows the factors are all the same number.

options.text: add the bases and add the indices
options.why: Treats the product as if the whole expression, base included, were being added.

questions.solution_text:
$3^{2}\times 3^{4}$
$=(3\times3)\times(3\times3\times3\times3)$
$=3^{6}$
Keep the base and add the indices: $a^{m}\times a^{n}=a^{m+n}$.

questions.question_text: For which expression does expanding produce one string of identical factors, so the index law of multiplication can be used?

options.why: Adding keeps two separate amounts, so the factors cannot be joined and counted.
The bases differ, so the expanded factors are not all the same number.
Added an index for the factor $2$ as though it were another power of $6$, but $2$ is not a power of the base, so the expanded factors are not all the same number.

questions.question_text: A student writes $2^{3}\times 2^{4}=4^{7}$. Expanding the product shows the correct single power is:

options.why: Added the indices correctly but also multiplied the two bases together.
Multiplied the indices instead of adding them.
Subtracted the indices as though the powers were being divided.

questions.question_text: $\left(7^{3}\right)^{4}$ can be written as the product $7^{3}\times 7^{3}\times 7^{3}\times 7^{3}$. Applying the index law of multiplication to that product gives:

options.why: Added the two indices in the bracket as $3+4$ instead of adding the index $3$ once for each of the four equal powers.
Added the index $3$ only three times, using the inner index as the number of equal powers.
Kept only the outer index and ignored the power inside the bracket.
